svg.text: Infusion rates: two formulas, and the sense-check that saves you
Drops per minute — gravity giving set
volume (mL) x drop factor
time (minutes)
Standard adult set = 20 drops/mL
Blood set = 15 drops/mL
Paediatric burette = 60 drops/mL
Millilitres per hour — infusion pump
total volume (mL)
time (hours)
1,000 mL over 8 hours = 125 mL/hour
A pump needs mL/hour. A gravity set needs
drops/minute. Know which you are setting.
Worked example — 1,000 mL over 8 hours, standard 20 drop set
Step 1 Convert the time to minutes: 8 x 60 = 480 minutes
Step 2 Multiply volume by drop factor: 1,000 x 20 = 20,000
Step 3 Divide: 20,000 / 480 = 41.7, so set about 42 drops per minute
Sense-check: a bag over 8 hours is 125 mL/h, roughly 2 mL a minute, so about 40 drops. 42 fits.
The decimal point rules that prevent tenfold errors
ALWAYS a leading zero: write 0.5 mg, never .5 mg — the dot is missed and 5 mg is given.
NEVER a trailing zero: write 5 mg, never 5.0 mg — read as 50 mg if the point is faint.
Write micrograms in full. The abbreviation is misread as mg — a thousandfold error.
If your answer needs more than one whole tablet-and-a-half, or more than 2 mL intramuscularly,
or a number that looks surprising — stop and recalculate before you draw it up.
